The International Astronomical Union (IAU) recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign 23 new names to impact craters on Mercury. The IAU has been the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors.

The newly named craters include:

\* Ailey, for Alvin Ailey (1931-1989), an American choreographer credited with popularizing modern dance and revolutionizing African-American participation in 20th century concert dance.

\* Aksakov, for Sergey Aksakov (1791-1859), a 19th-century Russian literary figure remembered for his semi-autobiographical tales of family life, as well as for his books on hunting and fishing.

\* Balanchine, for George Balanchine (1904-1983), one of the 20th century’s most famous choreographers, a developer of ballet in the United States and the co-founder and ballet master of New York City Ballet; he wrote more than 400 ballets.

\* Ellington, for Edward Kennedy “Duke” Ellington (1899-1974), an American composer, pianist, and big-band leader who, over the course of a 50-year career, wrote more than 1,000 compositions. A major figure in the history of jazz, he also wrote music that stretched into other genres, including blues, gospel, film scores, popular, and classical.

\* Faulkner, for William Faulkner (1897-1962), considered one of the most important writers of U.S. Southern literature. A Nobel Prize laureate, he worked in a variety of media but is best known for his novels and short stories.

\* Fonteyn, for Margot Fonteyn (1919-1991), an English ballerina regarded as one of the greatest classical ballet dancers of all time. She spent her entire career as a dancer with the Royal Ballet, eventually being appointed “Prima Ballerina Assoluta” of the company by Queen Elizabeth II.

\* Grainger, for Percy Grainger (1882-1961), an Australian-born composer, arranger, and pianist who, during the course of a 65-year career, played a prominent role in the revival of interest in British folk music in the early years of the 20th century.

\* Grotell, for Maija Grotell (1899-1973), a Finland-born ceramist and teacher known for her experiments in glaze technology and sometimes described as the “mother of American ceramics.”

\* Henri, for Robert Henri (1865-1929), an American painter and teacher. He was a leading figure of the Ashcan School, an early 20th century artistic movement best known for works portraying scenes of daily life in New York’s poorer neighborhoods.

\* Holst, for Gustav Theodore Holst (1874-1934), an English composer most famous for his orchestral suite, ‘The Planets”.

\* Kofi, for Vincent Akwete Kofi (1923-1974), a Ghanaian sculptor who borrowed extensively from traditional African concepts of stylization, emphasis, distortion and symbolism.

\* Lismer, for Arthur Lismer (1885-1969), a Canadian painter and member of the Group of Seven, a team of artists famous for its paintings inspired by the Canadian landscape and for initiating the first major Canadian national art movement.

\* Magritte, for Rene Magritte (1898-1967), a Belgian artist and one of the most prominent Surrealist painters, whose works were characterized by particular symbols, including the female torso, the bowler hat, the castle, the rock, and the window.

\* Mendelssohn, for Jakob Ludwig Felix Mendelssohn (1809-1847), a German composer, pianist, organist, and conductor of the early Romantic period. Among his most famous works is “Overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream”, which includes the “Wedding March”.

\* Nabokov, for Vladimir Nabokov (1899-1977), a multilingual Russian writer. He wrote his first literary works in Russian, but rose to international prominence for the novels he composed in English; his “Lolita” is frequently cited as one of the most important novels of the 20th century.

\* Nureyev, for Rudolf Nureyev (1938-1993), a Russian dancer, considered one of the most celebrated ballet dancers of the 20th century and credited with expanding the role to the male ballet dancer who once served only as support to the women.

\* Pasch, for Ulrica Fredrica Pasch (1735-1796), a Swedish painter and miniaturist and one of the few female artists known in Scandinavia before the 19th century. She was a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts.

\* Petipa, for Marius Petipa (1818-1910), a French ballet dancer, teacher and choreographer considered to be the most influential ballet master and choreographer of ballet that has ever lived.

\* Rustaveli, for Shota Rustaveli (1172-1216), a Georgian poet of the 12th century, and one of the greatest contributors to Georgian literature. He is author of “The Knight in the Panther’s Skin”, the Georgian national epic poem.

\* Seuss, for Theodor Seuss Geisel (1904-1991), an American writer and cartoonist most widely known for his 46 children’s books written under the pen names Dr. Seuss, Theo LeSieg, and, in one case, Rosetta Stone.

\* Sousa, for John Philip Sousa (1854-1932), an American composer and conductor of the late Romantic era, known particularly for American military and patriotic marches.

\* Stevenson, for Robert Louis Stevenson (1850-1894), a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist, and travel writer. His best-known books include “Treasure Island”, “Kidnapped”, and “The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde”.

\* Warhol, for Andy Warhol (1928-1987), a leading figure in the visual art movement known as pop art. His works explore the relationship between artistic expression, celebrity culture, and advertisement.

“The MESSENGER team is delighted that these geologically important features on Mercury now have official names,” says MESSENGER Principal Investigator Sean Solomon of the Carnegie Institution of Washington. “As these names appear regularly in the scientific literature and on maps of the innermost planet, the scientific community and the public will have many occasions to remember the brilliant individuals from many cultures whose contributions to the arts have enriched the lives of all.”

These 23 newly named craters join 53 other craters named since MESSENGER’s first Mercury flyby in January 2008. More information about the names of features on Mercury and the other objects in the Solar System can be found at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Planetary Nomenclature Web site: <http://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/index.html>.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Dr. Seuss, Alvin Ailey among the Names Selected for 23 Mercury Craters

by [SpaceRef](https://spacenews.com/author/spaceref/)

* [Share on X (Opens in new window) X](https://spacenews.com/dr-seuss-alvin-ailey-among-the-names-selected-for-23-mercury-craters/)

The International Astronomical Union (IAU) recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign 23 new names to impact craters on Mercury. The IAU has been the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors.

The newly named craters include:

\* Ailey, for Alvin Ailey (1931-1989), an American choreographer credited with popularizing modern dance and revolutionizing African-American participation in 20th century concert dance.

\* Aksakov, for Sergey Aksakov (1791-1859), a 19th-century Russian literary figure remembered for his semi-autobiographical tales of family life, as well as for his books on hunting and fishing.

\* Balanchine, for George Balanchine (1904-1983), one of the 20th century’s most famous choreographers, a developer of ballet in the United States and the co-founder and ballet master of New York City Ballet; he wrote more than 400 ballets.

\* Ellington, for Edward Kennedy “Duke” Ellington (1899-1974), an American composer, pianist, and big-band leader who, over the course of a 50-year career, wrote more than 1,000 compositions. A major figure in the history of jazz, he also wrote music that stretched into other genres, including blues, gospel, film scores, popular, and classical.

\* Faulkner, for William Faulkner (1897-1962), considered one of the most important writers of U.S. Southern literature. A Nobel Prize laureate, he worked in a variety of media but is best known for his novels and short stories.

\* Fonteyn, for Margot Fonteyn (1919-1991), an English ballerina regarded as one of the greatest classical ballet dancers of all time. She spent her entire career as a dancer with the Royal Ballet, eventually being appointed “Prima Ballerina Assoluta” of the company by Queen Elizabeth II.

\* Grainger, for Percy Grainger (1882-1961), an Australian-born composer, arranger, and pianist who, during the course of a 65-year career, played a prominent role in the revival of interest in British folk music in the early years of the 20th century.

\* Grotell, for Maija Grotell (1899-1973), a Finland-born ceramist and teacher known for her experiments in glaze technology and sometimes described as the “mother of American ceramics.”

\* Henri, for Robert Henri (1865-1929), an American painter and teacher. He was a leading figure of the Ashcan School, an early 20th century artistic movement best known for works portraying scenes of daily life in New York’s poorer neighborhoods.

\* Holst, for Gustav Theodore Holst (1874-1934), an English composer most famous for his orchestral suite, ‘The Planets”.

\* Kofi, for Vincent Akwete Kofi (1923-1974), a Ghanaian sculptor who borrowed extensively from traditional African concepts of stylization, emphasis, distortion and symbolism.

\* Lismer, for Arthur Lismer (1885-1969), a Canadian painter and member of the Group of Seven, a team of artists famous for its paintings inspired by the Canadian landscape and for initiating the first major Canadian national art movement.

\* Magritte, for Rene Magritte (1898-1967), a Belgian artist and one of the most prominent Surrealist painters, whose works were characterized by particular symbols, including the female torso, the bowler hat, the castle, the rock, and the window.

\* Mendelssohn, for Jakob Ludwig Felix Mendelssohn (1809-1847), a German composer, pianist, organist, and conductor of the early Romantic period. Among his most famous works is “Overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream”, which includes the “Wedding March”.

\* Nabokov, for Vladimir Nabokov (1899-1977), a multilingual Russian writer. He wrote his first literary works in Russian, but rose to international prominence for the novels he composed in English; his “Lolita” is frequently cited as one of the most important novels of the 20th century.

\* Nureyev, for Rudolf Nureyev (1938-1993), a Russian dancer, considered one of the most celebrated ballet dancers of the 20th century and credited with expanding the role to the male ballet dancer who once served only as support to the women.

\* Pasch, for Ulrica Fredrica Pasch (1735-1796), a Swedish painter and miniaturist and one of the few female artists known in Scandinavia before the 19th century. She was a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts.

\* Petipa, for Marius Petipa (1818-1910), a French ballet dancer, teacher and choreographer considered to be the most influential ballet master and choreographer of ballet that has ever lived.

\* Rustaveli, for Shota Rustaveli (1172-1216), a Georgian poet of the 12th century, and one of the greatest contributors to Georgian literature. He is author of “The Knight in the Panther’s Skin”, the Georgian national epic poem.

\* Seuss, for Theodor Seuss Geisel (1904-1991), an American writer and cartoonist most widely known for his 46 children’s books written under the pen names Dr. Seuss, Theo LeSieg, and, in one case, Rosetta Stone.

\* Sousa, for John Philip Sousa (1854-1932), an American composer and conductor of the late Romantic era, known particularly for American military and patriotic marches.

\* Stevenson, for Robert Louis Stevenson (1850-1894), a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist, and travel writer. His best-known books include “Treasure Island”, “Kidnapped”, and “The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde”.

\* Warhol, for Andy Warhol (1928-1987), a leading figure in the visual art movement known as pop art. His works explore the relationship between artistic expression, celebrity culture, and advertisement.

“The MESSENGER team is delighted that these geologically important features on Mercury now have official names,” says MESSENGER Principal Investigator Sean Solomon of the Carnegie Institution of Washington. “As these names appear regularly in the scientific literature and on maps of the innermost planet, the scientific community and the public will have many occasions to remember the brilliant individuals from many cultures whose contributions to the arts have enriched the lives of all.”

These 23 newly named craters join 53 other craters named since MESSENGER’s first Mercury flyby in January 2008. More information about the names of features on Mercury and the other objects in the Solar System can be found at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Planetary Nomenclature Web site: <http://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/index.html>.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)

* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Dr. Seuss, Alvin Ailey among the Names Selected for 23 Mercury Craters

by [SpaceRef](https://spacenews.com/author/spaceref/)

* [Share on X (Opens in new window) X](https://spacenews.com/dr-seuss-alvin-ailey-among-the-names-selected-for-23-mercury-craters/)

The International Astronomical Union (IAU) recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign 23 new names to impact craters on Mercury. The IAU has been the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors.

The newly named craters include:

\* Ailey, for Alvin Ailey (1931-1989), an American choreographer credited with popularizing modern dance and revolutionizing African-American participation in 20th century concert dance.

\* Aksakov, for Sergey Aksakov (1791-1859), a 19th-century Russian literary figure remembered for his semi-autobiographical tales of family life, as well as for his books on hunting and fishing.

\* Balanchine, for George Balanchine (1904-1983), one of the 20th century’s most famous choreographers, a developer of ballet in the United States and the co-founder and ballet master of New York City Ballet; he wrote more than 400 ballets.

\* Ellington, for Edward Kennedy “Duke” Ellington (1899-1974), an American composer, pianist, and big-band leader who, over the course of a 50-year career, wrote more than 1,000 compositions. A major figure in the history of jazz, he also wrote music that stretched into other genres, including blues, gospel, film scores, popular, and classical.

\* Faulkner, for William Faulkner (1897-1962), considered one of the most important writers of U.S. Southern literature. A Nobel Prize laureate, he worked in a variety of media but is best known for his novels and short stories.

\* Fonteyn, for Margot Fonteyn (1919-1991), an English ballerina regarded as one of the greatest classical ballet dancers of all time. She spent her entire career as a dancer with the Royal Ballet, eventually being appointed “Prima Ballerina Assoluta” of the company by Queen Elizabeth II.

\* Grainger, for Percy Grainger (1882-1961), an Australian-born composer, arranger, and pianist who, during the course of a 65-year career, played a prominent role in the revival of interest in British folk music in the early years of the 20th century.

\* Grotell, for Maija Grotell (1899-1973), a Finland-born ceramist and teacher known for her experiments in glaze technology and sometimes described as the “mother of American ceramics.”

\* Henri, for Robert Henri (1865-1929), an American painter and teacher. He was a leading figure of the Ashcan School, an early 20th century artistic movement best known for works portraying scenes of daily life in New York’s poorer neighborhoods.

\* Holst, for Gustav Theodore Holst (1874-1934), an English composer most famous for his orchestral suite, ‘The Planets”.

\* Kofi, for Vincent Akwete Kofi (1923-1974), a Ghanaian sculptor who borrowed extensively from traditional African concepts of stylization, emphasis, distortion and symbolism.

\* Lismer, for Arthur Lismer (1885-1969), a Canadian painter and member of the Group of Seven, a team of artists famous for its paintings inspired by the Canadian landscape and for initiating the first major Canadian national art movement.

\* Magritte, for Rene Magritte (1898-1967), a Belgian artist and one of the most prominent Surrealist painters, whose works were characterized by particular symbols, including the female torso, the bowler hat, the castle, the rock, and the window.

\* Mendelssohn, for Jakob Ludwig Felix Mendelssohn (1809-1847), a German composer, pianist, organist, and conductor of the early Romantic period. Among his most famous works is “Overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream”, which includes the “Wedding March”.

\* Nabokov, for Vladimir Nabokov (1899-1977), a multilingual Russian writer. He wrote his first literary works in Russian, but rose to international prominence for the novels he composed in English; his “Lolita” is frequently cited as one of the most important novels of the 20th century.

\* Nureyev, for Rudolf Nureyev (1938-1993), a Russian dancer, considered one of the most celebrated ballet dancers of the 20th century and credited with expanding the role to the male ballet dancer who once served only as support to the women.

\* Pasch, for Ulrica Fredrica Pasch (1735-1796), a Swedish painter and miniaturist and one of the few female artists known in Scandinavia before the 19th century. She was a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts.

\* Petipa, for Marius Petipa (1818-1910), a French ballet dancer, teacher and choreographer considered to be the most influential ballet master and choreographer of ballet that has ever lived.

\* Rustaveli, for Shota Rustaveli (1172-1216), a Georgian poet of the 12th century, and one of the greatest contributors to Georgian literature. He is author of “The Knight in the Panther’s Skin”, the Georgian national epic poem.

\* Seuss, for Theodor Seuss Geisel (1904-1991), an American writer and cartoonist most widely known for his 46 children’s books written under the pen names Dr. Seuss, Theo LeSieg, and, in one case, Rosetta Stone.

\* Sousa, for John Philip Sousa (1854-1932), an American composer and conductor of the late Romantic era, known particularly for American military and patriotic marches.

\* Stevenson, for Robert Louis Stevenson (1850-1894), a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist, and travel writer. His best-known books include “Treasure Island”, “Kidnapped”, and “The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde”.

\* Warhol, for Andy Warhol (1928-1987), a leading figure in the visual art movement known as pop art. His works explore the relationship between artistic expression, celebrity culture, and advertisement.

“The MESSENGER team is delighted that these geologically important features on Mercury now have official names,” says MESSENGER Principal Investigator Sean Solomon of the Carnegie Institution of Washington. “As these names appear regularly in the scientific literature and on maps of the innermost planet, the scientific community and the public will have many occasions to remember the brilliant individuals from many cultures whose contributions to the arts have enriched the lives of all.”

These 23 newly named craters join 53 other craters named since MESSENGER’s first Mercury flyby in January 2008. More information about the names of features on Mercury and the other objects in the Solar System can be found at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Planetary Nomenclature Web site: <http://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/index.html>.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

You are a web search agent. Follow your search method.

## Search method v006

Define both predicates precisely, including entity unit, eligible subtypes, exclusions and effective dates. Start sequentially with one X search, one Y search and one conjunction search. Maintain deduplicated dual frontiers and a ledger of canonical identities, aliases, evidence for each predicate, unresolved facts and estimated next-action cost. Group pending candidates into meaningful cohorts by their discovery source or eligibility subtype; do not invent arbitrary cohorts when none are useful. Separate evidence-backed near-intersections from speculative candidates that satisfy only one predicate. Resolve near-intersections first. For a speculative cohort, check at most three diverse candidates before committing more spend, and limit each dispatch to 10% of the initial budget; a single necessary check may exceed that cap if affordable. Inspect returned evidence before dispatching another sample. If a sample yields no verified addition or materially improved evidence, park that cohort and test another partition or the reverse frontier. No-hit candidates remain unresolved, not rejected. Revisit a parked cohort when new evidence, an alias or a demonstrably different source gives a better resolution path; a failed sample never proves the cohort empty. Expand productive cohorts in similarly small rounds, comparing verified additions and evidence progress per actual spend against discovery alternatives. Retain one neglected-cohort or reverse-frontier probe after two productive rounds so early samples do not permanently starve rare subtypes. After two discovery queries add no plausible identities, change source, subtype or frontier rather than paraphrasing the conjunction. Reuse established facts and never repeat settled checks. Keep at least 35% of initial budget for verification and evidence resolution, and stop discovery earlier if the promising pending queue requires it. End with identity, scope and date checks; submit only individually supported intersections and do not infer completeness from sampling or search saturation.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['parallel'].
Use Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for discovery and 4 for exact-name checks and first-pass check_candidates. Request identity-matched evidence for both tests while directing retrieval to the missing fact. Estimate dispatch cost per candidate and provider, not per tool invocation; fewer results are not presumed cheaper. Escalate only individual promising unresolved cases to Exa alone with 4 results after a cheap check or targeted fetch fails; never escalate a whole cohort because one member is ambiguous. Following baseline sampling and genuine Parallel stagnation, allow one Exa discovery probe on the weaker frontier if the resolution reserve remains intact; retain Exa discovery only for useful incremental evidence or identities. No broad auto-routing or routine concurrent variants. Domain filters belong on targeted evidence checks, with relaxation when necessary, not the entire discovery frontier. Use publication-date filters only when publication date defines eligibility; check effective dates in source content.

### Fetch policy
Cache facts and URLs. Fetch when source content can resolve a material identity or predicate uncertainty, or a discovered list supplies several plausible candidates. # Kennedy Center Honors

The **Kennedy Center Honors** is an annual tribute recognizing [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts") contributions to [American culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States"). Presented annually since 1978, a December gala celebrates five honorees at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center") Opera House in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[1]](#cite_note-about-1) Chiefly awarded to individuals for lifetime achievements, honorees have occasionally included duos or musical groups, while collective honors have recognized one [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theatre "Musical theatre"), one [television show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show"), and one performing arts venue.[[2]](#cite_note-WaPo_2024-2)

## Contents

## History

[George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") created the Kennedy Center Honors with [Nick Vanoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Vanoff "Nick Vanoff") and produced the first gala in 1978. He was the producer and co-writer through the 2014 awards,[[3]](#cite_note-3) after which he sold the production rights to the Kennedy Center.

The idea for the Kennedy Center Honors began in 1977, after that year's 10th-anniversary White House reception and Kennedy Center program for the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") (AFI). [Roger L. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_L._Stevens "Roger L. Stevens"), the founding chairman of the Kennedy Center, asked George Stevens Jr. (no relation), the founding director of the AFI, to hold an event for the center. Stevens Jr. asked Isaac Stern to become involved, and then pitched the idea to the television network [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS"), who bought it. With the first Honors event and honorees, CBS vice president for specials, Bernie Sofronski, stated:[[4]](#cite_note-wash_post-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

George [Stevens] came to us with this. What turned us on is that this is the only show of its kind. In Europe and most countries, they have ways of honoring their actors and their athletes. England has its command performances for the queen. We see this as a national honoring of people who have contributed to society, not someone who happens to have a pop record hit at the moment ... Our intention is not to do just another award show. We're going to make an effort in terms of a real special.

The first host was [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") in 1978, followed by [Eric Sevareid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sevareid "Eric Sevareid") in 1979 (with [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly") closing it) and [Beverly Sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Sills "Beverly Sills") in 1980. [Walter Cronkite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite "Walter Cronkite") hosted from 1981 to 2002 and [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") hosted from 2003 to 2012. [Glenn Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Close "Glenn Close") hosted in 2013 and [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert "Stephen Colbert") hosted from 2014 to 2016.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") and [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") of White Cherry Entertainment were the Executive Producers of the 38th annual Kennedy Center Honors (2015) after George Stevens Jr. stepped down.[[8]](#cite_note-8) There was no formal host in 2017, although Caroline Kennedy delivered an introduction. In 2018, mid-2021, and 2023 [Gloria Estefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Estefan "Gloria Estefan") hosted, [LL Cool J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LL_Cool_J "LL Cool J") hosted in 2019, and [David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Letterman "David Letterman") hosted in late 2021. Queen Latifah hosted in 2024. There was no formal host in 2022, though several former honorees delivered an introduction. In 2022, David Jammy of Done+Dusted and Elizabeth Kelly of ROK Productions were hired to serve as Executive Producers.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

This awards show does not air live (with the exception of closed-circuit venues), but an edited version lasting approximately two hours is normally televised on CBS after Christmas. In 2024, the presentation added a half hour, making the show two and a half hours.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) Normally, the show has been aired between Christmas and New Year's on CBS television, but, in a departure from this tradition, the 2019 Kennedy Center Honors aired on regular television in early December and was later made available on CBS All Access. Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the 2020 edition was postponed[[12]](#cite_note-12) and eventually held between May 17 and May 22, 2021, and the edited broadcast aired on June 6, 2021.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Since 2021, the annual Honors broadcast has been available to stream for a limited time through CBS platforms and Paramount+[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The 2025 Kennedy Center Honors ceremony, held at the Kennedy Center on December 7, 2025, was hosted by U.S. president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), thus marking the first time any sitting or former U.S. president hosted the Kennedy Center Honors.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

### Selection process

Honoree recommendations are accepted from the general public,[[17]](#cite_note-17) and the Kennedy Center initiated a Special Honors Advisory Committee, which comprises members of the board of trustees as well as past honorees and distinguished artists.[[18]](#cite_note-18) The executive committee of the board of trustees selects the honoree recipients based on their impact and contributions to American culture and excellence in music, dance, theater, opera, motion pictures or television.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The selections are typically announced sometime between July and September. Most honorees are [Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans"), with non-U.S. citizen honorees typically hailing from elsewhere in the [anglosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere "Anglosphere").

## Events

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg/250px-Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

The invitation-only, weekend-long ceremony includes the Chairman's Luncheon, the State Department dinner, White House reception, and the Honors gala performances and supper.

The Chairman's Luncheon is held on Saturday at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center"). Surrounded by the honorees, the chairman of the board of trustees launches the event with a welcoming speech. At that evening's reception and dinner at the [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), presided over by the [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), the honorees are introduced and the Honors medallions are presented by the chairman of the board.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The wide rainbow-colored ribbon then hung around the necks of the recipients and prominently noticeable when the events are televised, symbolizes "a spectrum of many skills within the performing arts" according to creator [Ivan Chermayeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chermayeff "Ivan Chermayeff").[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

On Sunday, there is an early-evening [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") reception,[[22]](#cite_note-22) traditionally hosted by the [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States"), followed by the Honors gala performance at the Kennedy Center and supper.

Prior to 2017, there had been three occasions in which the president did not attend the gala performance. President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") did not attend in 1979 during the [Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"); First Lady [Rosalynn Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalynn_Carter "Rosalynn Carter") served as his surrogate.[[23]](#cite_note-23) President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") was on a trip to [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") and could not attend in 1989; First Lady [Barbara Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Bush "Barbara Bush") served as his surrogate.[[24]](#cite_note-24) President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") was on a trip to [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest") and could not attend in 1994; First Lady [Hillary Rodham Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Rodham_Clinton "Hillary Rodham Clinton") served as his surrogate.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

For the 2015 gala performance, President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") joined First Lady [Michelle Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Obama "Michelle Obama") late after addressing the nation in a live telecast from the White House.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

In 2017, President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and First Lady [Melania Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melania_Trump "Melania Trump") decided not to participate in events honoring recipients of the 2017 Kennedy Center Honors awards to "allow the Honorees to celebrate without any political distraction."[[27]](#cite_note-27) The 2017 ceremony was held on December 3, 2017, without them, marking the first time that neither the president nor the first lady attended; [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") was the host and presented the honorees. The traditional dinner at the State Department on the Saturday evening before the ceremony was hosted by [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") [Rex Tillerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Tillerson "Rex Tillerson"), and the White House reception was canceled.[[28]](#cite_note-2017gala-28) Donald and Melania Trump also did not participate in any of the events of the 2018 or 2019 editions.[[29]](#cite_note-var-9dec2019-29)

Because of changes imposed on the delayed and abbreviated 2020 edition due to the COVID-19 pandemic, President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and First Lady [Jill Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Biden "Jill Biden") welcomed that year's honorees to the White House in May 2021 but did not attend any other events.

For the 2021 edition, Joe and Jill Biden attended the gala performance on December 5, 2021, marking the first time since 2016 that a sitting president and first lady had attended the event.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

In 2025, the medallion given to each recipient received a redesign by [Tiffany & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiffany_&_Co. "Tiffany & Co.") for the first time since 1978. The former design from James "Jimmy" Baturin had rainbow ribbons and a gold name plate. The new design has a navy blue strap holding the gold disc, which includes the building and the rainbow colors.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

Also in 2025, after the board of the center made the decision to change the name, CBS added a voiceover to relabel the annual honors as "Trump-Kennedy Center Honors".[[32]](#cite_note-Trump-32) Trump hosted the ceremony himself, the first time a president has done so[[33]](#cite_note-33), and the [Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_Media_Research "Nielsen Media Research") ratings for broadcast dropped to a new all-time low.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

As of 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit), 268 people have been awarded the Kennedy Center Honors, as well as two special awards.[[35]](#cite_note-35) The award given to stand-up comedian and actor [Bill Cosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby "Bill Cosby") in 1998 was rescinded in 2018 following Cosby's sexual assault conviction.[[36]](#cite_note-cosbyrescind-36)

The vast majority of Kennedy Center Honors have been bestowed on individuals. On 13 occasions since 1985, awards have been presented to duos or groups, including three married couples who were actors: [Hume Cronyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hume_Cronyn "Hume Cronyn") and [Jessica Tandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Tandy "Jessica Tandy"); [Paul Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Newman "Paul Newman") and [Joanne Woodward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joanne_Woodward "Joanne Woodward"); and [Ossie Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossie_Davis "Ossie Davis") and [Ruby Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_Dee "Ruby Dee"). Dancers The [Nicholas Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Brothers "Nicholas Brothers"), Fayard and Harold were honored, along with three [musical theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theater "Musical theater") songwriting duos: [Alan Jay Lerner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Jay_Lerner "Alan Jay Lerner") and [Frederick Loewe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Loewe "Frederick Loewe"), [Betty Comden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Comden "Betty Comden") and [Adolph Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolph_Green "Adolph Green"), and [John Kander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kander "John Kander") and [Fred Ebb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Ebb "Fred Ebb").

Members of seven music groups were awarded: [Pete Townshend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Townshend "Pete Townshend") and [Roger Daltrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Daltrey "Roger Daltrey") of [The Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who"); [John Paul Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Paul_Jones_(musician) "John Paul Jones (musician)"), [Jimmy Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Page "Jimmy Page") and [Robert Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Plant "Robert Plant") of [Led Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin "Led Zeppelin"); [Don Henley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Henley "Don Henley"), [Timothy B. # Dr. Seuss, Alvin Ailey among the Names Selected for 23 Mercury Craters

by [SpaceRef](https://spacenews.com/author/spaceref/)

* [Share on X (Opens in new window) X](https://spacenews.com/dr-seuss-alvin-ailey-among-the-names-selected-for-23-mercury-craters/)
* [Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn](https://spacenews.com/dr-seuss-alvin-ailey-among-the-names-selected-for-23-mercury-craters/)

* [Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email](mailto:?subject=%5BShared%20Post%5D%20Dr.%20Seuss%2C%20Alvin%20Ailey%20among%20the%20Names%20Selected%20for%2023%20Mercury%20Craters&body=https%3A%2F%2Fspacenews.com%2Fdr-seuss-alvin-ailey-among-the-names-selected-for-23-mercury-craters%2F&share=email&nb=1)

  

The International Astronomical Union (IAU) recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign 23 new names to impact craters on Mercury. The IAU has been the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors.

The newly named craters include:

\* Ailey, for Alvin Ailey (1931-1989), an American choreographer credited with popularizing modern dance and revolutionizing African-American participation in 20th century concert dance.

\* Aksakov, for Sergey Aksakov (1791-1859), a 19th-century Russian literary figure remembered for his semi-autobiographical tales of family life, as well as for his books on hunting and fishing.

\* Balanchine, for George Balanchine (1904-1983), one of the 20th century’s most famous choreographers, a developer of ballet in the United States and the co-founder and ballet master of New York City Ballet; he wrote more than 400 ballets.

\* Ellington, for Edward Kennedy “Duke” Ellington (1899-1974), an American composer, pianist, and big-band leader who, over the course of a 50-year career, wrote more than 1,000 compositions. A major figure in the history of jazz, he also wrote music that stretched into other genres, including blues, gospel, film scores, popular, and classical.

\* Faulkner, for William Faulkner (1897-1962), considered one of the most important writers of U.S. Southern literature. A Nobel Prize laureate, he worked in a variety of media but is best known for his novels and short stories.

\* Fonteyn, for Margot Fonteyn (1919-1991), an English ballerina regarded as one of the greatest classical ballet dancers of all time. She spent her entire career as a dancer with the Royal Ballet, eventually being appointed “Prima Ballerina Assoluta” of the company by Queen Elizabeth II.

\* Grainger, for Percy Grainger (1882-1961), an Australian-born composer, arranger, and pianist who, during the course of a 65-year career, played a prominent role in the revival of interest in British folk music in the early years of the 20th century.

\* Grotell, for Maija Grotell (1899-1973), a Finland-born ceramist and teacher known for her experiments in glaze technology and sometimes described as the “mother of American ceramics.”

\* Henri, for Robert Henri (1865-1929), an American painter and teacher. He was a leading figure of the Ashcan School, an early 20th century artistic movement best known for works portraying scenes of daily life in New York’s poorer neighborhoods.

\* Holst, for Gustav Theodore Holst (1874-1934), an English composer most famous for his orchestral suite, ‘The Planets”.

\* Kofi, for Vincent Akwete Kofi (1923-1974), a Ghanaian sculptor who borrowed extensively from traditional African concepts of stylization, emphasis, distortion and symbolism.

\* Lismer, for Arthur Lismer (1885-1969), a Canadian painter and member of the Group of Seven, a team of artists famous for its paintings inspired by the Canadian landscape and for initiating the first major Canadian national art movement.

\* Magritte, for Rene Magritte (1898-1967), a Belgian artist and one of the most prominent Surrealist painters, whose works were characterized by particular symbols, including the female torso, the bowler hat, the castle, the rock, and the window.

\* Mendelssohn, for Jakob Ludwig Felix Mendelssohn (1809-1847), a German composer, pianist, organist, and conductor of the early Romantic period. Among his most famous works is “Overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream”, which includes the “Wedding March”.

\* Nabokov, for Vladimir Nabokov (1899-1977), a multilingual Russian writer. He wrote his first literary works in Russian, but rose to international prominence for the novels he composed in English; his “Lolita” is frequently cited as one of the most important novels of the 20th century.

\* Nureyev, for Rudolf Nureyev (1938-1993), a Russian dancer, considered one of the most celebrated ballet dancers of the 20th century and credited with expanding the role to the male ballet dancer who once served only as support to the women.

\* Pasch, for Ulrica Fredrica Pasch (1735-1796), a Swedish painter and miniaturist and one of the few female artists known in Scandinavia before the 19th century. She was a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts.

\* Petipa, for Marius Petipa (1818-1910), a French ballet dancer, teacher and choreographer considered to be the most influential ballet master and choreographer of ballet that has ever lived.

\* Rustaveli, for Shota Rustaveli (1172-1216), a Georgian poet of the 12th century, and one of the greatest contributors to Georgian literature. He is author of “The Knight in the Panther’s Skin”, the Georgian national epic poem.

\* Seuss, for Theodor Seuss Geisel (1904-1991), an American writer and cartoonist most widely known for his 46 children’s books written under the pen names Dr. Seuss, Theo LeSieg, and, in one case, Rosetta Stone.

\* Sousa, for John Philip Sousa (1854-1932), an American composer and conductor of the late Romantic era, known particularly for American military and patriotic marches.

\* Stevenson, for Robert Louis Stevenson (1850-1894), a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist, and travel writer. His best-known books include “Treasure Island”, “Kidnapped”, and “The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde”.

\* Warhol, for Andy Warhol (1928-1987), a leading figure in the visual art movement known as pop art. His works explore the relationship between artistic expression, celebrity culture, and advertisement.

“The MESSENGER team is delighted that these geologically important features on Mercury now have official names,” says MESSENGER Principal Investigator Sean Solomon of the Carnegie Institution of Washington. “As these names appear regularly in the scientific literature and on maps of the innermost planet, the scientific community and the public will have many occasions to remember the brilliant individuals from many cultures whose contributions to the arts have enriched the lives of all.”

These 23 newly named craters join 53 other craters named since MESSENGER’s first Mercury flyby in January 2008. More information about the names of features on Mercury and the other objects in the Solar System can be found at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Planetary Nomenclature Web site: <http://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/index.html>.

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.
